title: How work runs: batches, dispatch, reviews, rulings

entries.summary: Merge fast-forward only, from the CLI, after aggregating the branch into clean logical commits. No merge commits, no GitHub squash merges.
body: Aggregate with `git reset --soft $(git merge-base main HEAD)` and recommit in one to five Conventional Commits when interactive rebase is not available.
The project skill `finishing-a-feature` is the procedure.

entries.summary: No commit that lands on main may fail the ci.yml checked in beside it; sequence a migration's deletions or collapse the red range at aggregation.
body: A fast-forward merge lands every aggregated commit on main; a bisect, a revert target, or a checkout of any of them must build and pass the CI definition at that same commit.

Batch 20 T3: the corpus deletion commits satisfied the cargo-side flip-with-deletion rule at every commit, but the still-present JS gate (corpus.test.mjs) was red from the first deletion commit until the vitest layer itself retired - caught only by the reviewer's per-commit reproduction, and repaired at aggregation by collapsing the range into the deletion commit.

The check at aggregation time: for each collapsed commit, the gates its own ci.yml names run green; a migration that cannot keep an interim gate green retires that gate's subject in the same collapsed commit.

source.ref: batch 20 branch review; task-3-review.json important finding 1; T3 report concerns[10]

entries.summary: Before a new gate or pipeline step ships, walk every commit author class and every generated resource it touches through it on paper; state each accepted red.
body: Batch 24 shipped a payload-stamp mechanism (tree gate + per-commit co-change + range co-change) proven against 40 human-authored commits, while release-please-config.json's own extra-files entry scheduled a bot commit to template/** that trips all three, plus the dogfood version-stamp test -- discovered only at the branch review.

The walk is cheap: enumerate the automation that writes commits to this repository (release-please, Dependabot, the restamp step), list the exact files each writes, and run the new check's predicate against those file sets.

Extended 2026-09-13 (owner, design.md 5.78): the walk covers generated RESOURCES too -- releases, tags, PRs -- with one named owner per resource. The T2 create-collision (design.md 5.77) was two automations both creating the v0.3.0 release object; the commit-class walk alone missed it the same day this rule shipped.
A check added to a shipped gate is walked through the installed populations, and the new predicate runs over the template at each release tag (design.md 183).

source.ref: batch 24 branch review issues 1-2; adopted standing at the batch-24 report (design.md 5.75)

entries.summary: Give a fix round to a fresh implementer with the tree state in its brief; a resumed implementer costs about three times the tokens per tool use.
body: Measured in batch 33: Task 5's round 2 on a resumed agent used 732,296 tokens, its round 3 on a fresh agent 163,693; Task 7's round 2c (resumed) used 7,338 tokens per tool use, round 2b (fresh) 2,138.
The brief names FIX_BASE, the findings with the review's own checks, and the controller's positions, so a fresh agent needs no earlier transcript.

source.ref: batch 33 branch review recommendation; progress.md usage rows

entries.summary: When a release spans several batches, its release-please PR stays unmerged until the last batch is on main; never offer it as a merge before then.
body: release-please opens the release PR as soon as main holds a release-worthy commit, so the PR exists from the first batch on and grows with each one.

The owner rules the hold in the release's meta-spec (design.md 5.99 for 2.0.0): the held PR is the only gate on adopters, and the last batch's branch review re-checks the release's coverage before it merges.
A batch close report lists the open release PR as held, with the batch that releases it; it never lists it as a merge to decide.

source.ref: owner correction at the batch-33 close; design.md 5.99

entries.summary: A spec's design review repeats with a fresh reviewer after each round that holds a Critical finding, until a round holds none.
body: Fix every finding of the round first. Important and Minor findings are folded into the spec without a further review (design.md 5.159).
The loop has no cap; the owner sees the spec only after a round with no Critical finding (design.md 178).

entries.summary: A GitHub repository created for a live run is private, and every later report names it with a reminder to delete it until the owner says it is gone.
body: The owner allows scratch repositories for live runs on these two conditions (design.md 180).
houserules and its agents never delete a repository; deleting is the owner's step. Record each repository's name and creation in the batch ledger.

entries.summary: A command the harness refuses is never run another way: no script, no wrapper. The agent stops that step, names it in its report, and hands it back.
body: The person who runs the work then runs the step in their own session, or asks the owner. A live run that needs a refused command, such as git in a scratch repository, goes back the same way.
Another way includes a shell glob or a variable that spells the refused command or its path differently, a script, and a wrapper.
Every brief carries this rule. A report that discloses a wrapped refused command is a review finding, and its captures count as unverified until the step is re-run by the person who runs the work.

One handed-back step the controller takes over: a `git commit` that the harness refused an agent in the agent's own worktree. The controller commits the agent's staged change with the message the agent wrote, then lets the agent finish its step (owner, 2026-10-21: "you should take over the committing because you are allowed to").

source.ref: owner ruling in chat, batch 34 (refused commands)

entries.summary: Haiku trial: from batch 37, give haiku at least one implementer task per batch, a level harder after each clean close; record it beside the sonnet tasks.
body: Intent (owner, 2026-10-23, verbatim): "I want you to give haiku increasingly difficult tasks during the next implementations and track how it performs. The intention here is to gauge if - through houserule's setup - models that you normally wouldn't use because they are not mighty enough are enabled to perform better through having clear, targeted rules."

Levels, by the task the plan describes: L1 a spec that fixes the exact output, few files, no interface that another task consumes; L2 new logic with its own tests, no interface that another task consumes; L3 an interface that a later task consumes; L4 a critical task (design.md 173). Batch 37 starts at L1.

Moves: after a haiku task closes with no Critical or Important finding and no more fix rounds than the median sonnet task of its batch, the next haiku task is one level higher; after one Important finding it stays at its level; after a Critical finding or two Important findings it drops one level (not below L1).

A haiku task gets the same brief, Knowledge ids, tier, review model, and review caps as a sonnet task of its level: the trial measures what the setup gives a smaller model, so it adds no extra help and lowers no gate.

Record: the dispatch's ledger row names the model, the level, and the reason; its close line states the review's findings by severity, the fix rounds, the re-reviews, and the token and tool-use counts the harness shows. At batch close, append one data point to HR-242 (batch, task, level, outcome, the same counts of the batch's sonnet tasks) and report it to the owner.

Gate (owner, 2026-10-23, design.md 5.225): after every fourth haiku data point in HR-242, and at once after any Critical finding on a haiku task, the controller takes the data table to the owner: haiku against the sonnet tasks of the same level, with findings by severity, fix rounds, re-reviews, tokens, and time. The owner rules continue, change the levels or the moves, stop, or make haiku the default up to a level. Until then a plan may give haiku two tasks per batch when it holds two at the current level.

Owner, 2026-10-21: "I want you to keep an eye on whether haiku brings enough quality as an implementer or if haiku provokes many review rounds. If Haiku is not a good fit, decide case-by-case if the task is simple enough for haiku or is sonnet should be used."

source.ref: owner rulings in chat, batch 34 (haiku implementer) and batch 36 (the haiku trial, design.md 5.224)

entries.summary: A commit that records a ruling, an acceptance, or a ledger fact names the work items it concerns; a ruling about no item files one first.
body: The every-commit trailer rule has no exemption for such a commit. An acceptance commit names the items of the accepted batches; a ruling commit names the items the ruling changes or books; a ruling that concerns no item files a work item before the commit that records it.
Owner ruling 2026-10-21 (batch 34 ruling sheet, trailer card): "Name the items it concerns".

entries.summary: A spec review under a meta-spec compares the spec against every section of the meta-spec and lists the sections it compared, with a coverage table.
body: The dispatch names the meta-spec and says to cover all of it: the goal, the method, the inventory rows, the batch row and its amendments, the interactions, every function row the batch touches, the upgrade path, this repository, the coverage check, every ruling, and the out-of-scope list. The review's scope lists each section it compared, and a coverage table maps each section to what binds the batch and where the spec carries it, or the gap.
Owner, 2026-10-22, verbatim: "The whole meta spec must be taken into account to be sure that nothing was missed."

entries.summary: Every batch measures its token and time cost per phase and per dispatch, so a later process change can be compared with an earlier batch.
body: Keep `<workspace>/efficiency-windows.json` current: one window (`phase`, `start`, `end`, UTC) per phase: spec, plan, each task wave with its reviews and fix rounds, the live run, and the branch review.

Run `python3 -I .superpowers/sdd/2026-10-10-batch-33/efficiency.py <workspace>` at each phase end and save the output as `<workspace>/efficiency.json`. It sums the controller's model usage (main-session assistant messages, each message id once) and the subagent dispatches that finished in each window (tokens, tool uses, duration), plus wall-clock time. Run it once more before the branch review dispatches, so that the branch reviewer reads the batch's `efficiency.json`.
Record every dispatch's tokens, tool uses, and duration from its completion notification in the ledger row that closes it.

The baseline is batch 33, the first full-tier batch measured this way, and `efficiency-baseline.json` (every dispatch of batches 28 to 33 that the transcripts hold; a dispatch whose call the transcripts lost has no role). Compare a later batch per phase and per dispatch with it, never as one total.
